doc.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Joining Basie and life on the road
title: Touring narrows; Las Vegas and the Dust Bowl
summary: The band's range shrank by the early 1960s, the South eased up, and in 1957 Las Vegas band members stayed in the Dust Bowl.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: How often did you tour the South? Was that something that happened as part of every year, or there just were particular years where this was a part of the focus?
It seemed as though it happened every year or every other year. As the years wore on our sphere of activity in the United States sort of narrowed, and we --
When was that perceptible that it was narrowing? In other words, when did you -­

In the late ’50s and early ’60s there were certain places that we seemed to travel to less. The western boundaries seemed to be around Kansas City or St. Louis and sometimes Omaha, Okalahoma City. Then from there we’d jump to Los Angeles and Seattle and San Diego.
Things started to get better in the South. We stayed at some hotels downtown as far as I can remember, during my latter period with the band.

Yeah. In ’57, when we first went to Las Vegas, the band members had to stay in a section of town called the Dust Bowl, which is tantamount to Las Vegas’s Harlem. They called it the Dust Bowl, because that’s just what it was. We couldn’t stay on The Strip, so to speak. We played on The Strip where the clubs would be, big hotels, the Flamingo, the Dunes, et cetera.
